lesson.title: The Gap Between Guess and Reality: Calculating Residuals
lesson.summary: A residual measures exactly how far off a regression line's prediction is for one real data point, and computing it is nothing more than subtraction.
lesson.body:
A regression line is a prediction machine. Feed it an x-value and it hands back a predicted y-value, written y-hat. But real data almost never lines up perfectly with a straight line, so every actual point sits a little above or a little below the line's prediction. The residual is the precise size of that miss for a single point: residual = observed y minus predicted y, or e = y - y-hat. Calculating a residual is just subtraction, but doing it carefully for every point is the first step in checking whether a line is actually doing a good job, and it is the building block for nearly every diagnostic tool covered later in regression analysis.

Suppose five students report hours studied (x) and exam score (y): (1, 55), (2, 65), (3, 70), (4, 80), (5, 88). Fitting a least-squares regression line to this data gives y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1x (the slope and intercept come from the usual least-squares formulas, which you calculate once you have a regression line in hand). To find residuals, plug each x into the equation to get a prediction, then subtract that prediction from the actual y. It helps to organize the work in a table with columns for x, observed y, predicted y-hat, and the residual, since that layout makes it easy to check every subtraction at a glance.

For x = 1: y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1(1) = 55.4, and the actual score was 55, so the residual is 55 - 55.4 = -0.4. For x = 2: y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1(2) = 63.5, actual 65, residual = 65 - 63.5 = 1.5. For x = 3: y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1(3) = 71.6, actual 70, residual = 70 - 71.6 = -1.6. For x = 4: y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1(4) = 79.7, actual 80, residual = 80 - 79.7 = 0.3. For x = 5: y-hat = 47.3 + 8.1(5) = 87.8, actual 88, residual = 88 - 87.8 = 0.2. Each of these five subtractions is independent of the others; a mistake in one row's arithmetic does not carry over into the next, which is exactly why organizing the calculation row by row keeps errors easy to catch.

The sign of a residual tells you which direction the line missed. A positive residual means the actual value sat above the line, so the model underestimated that point. A negative residual means the actual value fell below the line, so the model overestimated. Here the student who studied 3 hours scored 1.6 points lower than predicted, while the student who studied 2 hours scored 1.5 points higher than predicted. Add up all five residuals: -0.4 + 1.5 - 1.6 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.0. That is not a coincidence. Because the least-squares line is built specifically to minimize the sum of squared residuals, the residuals always sum to (essentially) zero, which is a handy arithmetic check on your work: if your five residuals do not sum close to zero, go back and check your slope and intercept before trusting any of the individual values.

Residuals are the raw material for almost everything else in regression diagnostics. Once you can calculate them point by point, you can plot them to look for patterns, square and sum them to measure overall fit, or watch how dramatically they shrink or grow when a single unusual point is added or removed. None of that is possible without first mastering this basic subtraction, so it is worth practicing until picking out y, y-hat, and the resulting residual becomes automatic, the same way learning to add fractions has to become automatic before you can tackle algebra built on top of it.
